article_title: Enhancing histology education: Iranian medical students' experience with eHistoLab web-application virtual microscopy.
citation: Poorhassan M, Hooshmandja M, Karimian Z, Seifali E. (2026). Enhancing histology education: Iranian medical students’ experience with eHistoLab web-application virtual microscopy. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09829-w
title: eHistoLab web application: a bilingual virtual microscopy platform for histology education
description: eHistoLab is an Iranian-developed mobile learning platform built at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences that applies virtual microscopy to histology education. It incorporates "a library of approximately 130 high-quality histological slides" digitized by whole-slide scanning, viewable at magnifications of up to ×400. Features include high-quality schematic images, public and private forums for exchanging with professors, Persian/English switching, a favorites section, search functionality for tissue structures, and instructor exchange during online training. It was published on Google Play after approval by the School of Medicine.
requirements: Access is restricted through individual usernames and passwords to prevent cross-group contamination in the study setting.
constraints: The study evaluated it only in a blended configuration together with recorded e-lectures, not as a standalone replacement for instruction.
target_learners: Medical, dentistry, and pharmacy students in preclinical histology courses
target_learning_goals: Recognition and interpretation of microscopic structures in histology
examples: In the study, the eHistoLab group used the application alongside identical recorded lectures on the LMS, while the comparison group received e-lecturing via Adobe Connect.

citation: Ernst S, Almorad A, Badertscher P, Duncker D, Gallagher AG, Li A, Nisbet A, De Ponti R, Porta-Sánchez A, Mont L, De Riva M, Sarkozy A, Schamroth N, Svennberg E, Tjong F, Trines SA, Vitali-Serdoz L, Boveda S. (2026). Digitally assisted learning in cardiac electrophysiology and cardiac implantable electronic devices: a Scientific Statement of the European Heart Rhythm Association of the ESC. Europace. https://doi.org/10.1093/europace/euag081
title: EHRA Simulation Village: a neutral, society-governed access model for comparing simulation modalities
description: The EHRA Simulation Village, launched in 2023, is a supervised environment in which trainees can compare simulation modalities and platforms under scientific society oversight, offering an alternative to industry-mediated access. The statement reports high acceptance by participants and positions the model as "a scalable blueprint, ideally evolving into regional hubs linked to standardized assessment and formal certification pathways". It is presented as one solution to the documented access gap, with broader initiatives still needed.
requirements: Scientific society oversight to preserve educational neutrality
Evolution into regional hubs linked to standardized assessment and formal certification pathways
target_learners: EP and CIED trainees across Europe
target_learning_goals: comparison of platforms under neutral governance
examples: Launched in 2023 at EHRA, the village provides supervised, society-governed access to multiple simulator platforms.

article_title: Short-Term Effects of an eHealth Care Experiential Learning Program Among Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Yu-Shan Cheng, Cheng-Pei Lin, Lu-Yen Anny Chen, Wei-Ren Hwang, Yi-Chun Lin, Yu-Chi Chen. (2024). Short-Term Effects of an eHealth Care Experiential Learning Program Among Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/53509
title: Six-session eHealth care experiential learning program for patients with type 2 diabetes
description: A 3-month program of "6 biweekly sessions over 3 months, each lasting around 90 minutes," developed over 3 years from a qualitative needs study and refined from 8 to 6 sessions after a Delphi study and pilot. Sessions combined theoretical knowledge with hands-on training and at-home practice using eHealth tools common in Taiwanese clinical settings, including wearable devices (Xiaomi), apps such as Health2Sync, LINE, and My Health Bank, and blood pressure and glucose monitors. Development cost was approximately US $66 including wearable devices and Bluetooth-enabled health monitors.
requirements: Participants need a mobile phone or tablet with an internet connection and the ability to communicate in Mandarin or Taiwanese
constraints: Developed and evaluated specifically for patients with type 2 diabetes receiving case management services in Taiwan
target_learners: Adults with type 2 diabetes receiving case management services
target_learning_goals: use of eHealth care technology for daily self-management
examples: Each session opened with 15 minutes of questions and feedback on the previous session, followed by content introduction and 15-20 minutes of assisted practical operation, with between-session coaching via a social media platform

article_title: Short-Term Effects of an eHealth Care Experiential Learning Program Among Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Yu-Shan Cheng, Cheng-Pei Lin, Lu-Yen Anny Chen, Wei-Ren Hwang, Yi-Chun Lin, Yu-Chi Chen. (2024). Short-Term Effects of an eHealth Care Experiential Learning Program Among Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: Randomized Controlled Trial. Journal of Medical Internet Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/53509
title: Six-session curriculum sequencing eHealth skills across the experiential learning cycle
description: The program's six sessions form a reusable lesson-level sequence: session 1 ("A new realm of health technology care") introduces smart health care functions and motivates engagement; session 2 ("Fighting against sugar") focuses on regular health monitoring and self-management with practice tools; session 3 addresses complications, particularly chronic kidney disease; session 4 ("eHealth care by your side") uses competitions and hands-on activities to foster independent operation; session 5 ("My smart eHealth in daily care") integrates smart health care into daily self-management; and session 6 ("My eHealth care practice journey") synthesizes and reviews all prior content with comprehensive hands-on practice.
requirements: Sessions need hands-on practice tools, wearable devices, and research-assistant support for practical operation
constraints: Content is diabetes-specific (blood sugar, blood pressure, diet monitoring; chronic kidney disease prevention)
target_learning_goals: integrating health technology into daily self-management
examples: Session 4 encouraged patients to operate the technology independently and discuss challenges, "facilitating learning from real-life experiences"
